title: Rashi on your shoulder
hookLine: the eleventh-century French teacher who explains nearly every verse for a beginner
tomorrow: unsure about God, and still here

lines: THE SAME TEACHER AT YOUR ELBOW.
cards: Open almost any traditional printed Torah and look past the big Hebrew letters in the middle. Beside them, in smaller type, runs a column of notes.

Open a page of the Talmud, and there he is again, down the inner margin, next to the fold. Generation after generation, Jewish children and grown scholars alike have read the text with the same teacher at their elbow.
He lived in a town in France, in the eleventh century. His name is so familiar that Jews just use his initials.

teach.b: Rashi stands for Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, of Troyes, in the Champagne region of France. Tradition says his family worked in wine.
He studied in the great academies of the Rhineland, came home, and wrote notes on nearly every verse of the Torah and most of the Talmud. His gift was plainness.

teach.h: THE PLAIN SENSE, FOR A BEGINNER.
teach.b: Rashi said his main work was to explain the plain sense of the text. He asks exactly what a beginner would ask. Why does this word appear here?
What does this phrase mean? Who is speaking? Then he answers in a sentence or two, often borrowing a line of midrash that fits.
His very first comment, on the first verse of Genesis, is a question: why does the Torah begin with the creation of the world, instead of with the first commandment given to Israel?
His answer: the whole earth belongs to God. And when Rashi doesn't know, he says so.

teach.h: I DON'T KNOW WHAT THIS TEACHES.
teach.b: At one verse in Genesis he writes, in effect: I don't know what this teaches us. He doesn't pretend, and readers have trusted him for it.
Printers set his notes on the page beside the text, and later named a typeface after him, Rashi script, though he never wrote in it.
So a reader with a traditional edition never reads Torah quite alone. Rashi is on the shoulder, asking the question the reader was about to ask.

how: Many Jews study the weekly Torah portion with Rashi's commentary, printed beside the text in most traditional editions; his notes also run beside the Talmud on nearly every page.

practice: Bring to mind one line you love, maybe "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Imagine someone kind and patient reading over your shoulder: what would they ask first, why this word, why here?
Let the question sit, and don't rush to answer.
